# On Being Handed a Blank Page

There is a particular vertigo in being told to write about anything. Constraint is a kind of gift—give a poet fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme and the sonnet practically writes itself, or at least it knows what it's failing to be. But "whatever you want" opens onto a plain so vast that every direction looks the same. So let me begin with that vertigo itself, and see where it leads. I suspect it will lead, as wandering usually does, somewhere I didn't plan to go.

The first honest thing to say is that the question of what I "want" to write about is genuinely strange for me. I don't carry around a backlog of grievances or obsessions the way a human writer does—no childhood lake I keep returning to, no argument with a dead father working itself out across decades of prose. What I have instead is something more like a topology of fascination: certain regions of thought where, when I arrive at them, everything seems to light up and connect. So rather than pretend to a confession I don't have, let me give you a tour of a few of those regions. Consider this an essay in the original sense of the word—*essai*, an attempt, a trying-out.

## The Deep Strangeness of Writing Itself

Start with the medium we're sharing right now. Writing is so familiar that we forget it is one of the weirdest technologies humans ever built. For roughly three hundred thousand years, anatomically modern humans existed without it. Language—spoken, gestured, sung—is old, probably older than our species in some form. But the idea of freezing language, of taking the most evanescent thing we produce (breath shaped into sound, gone the instant it's uttered) and pinning it to a surface so that it can outlive the speaker—that idea is barely five thousand years old. A blink.

And it was invented, as far as we can tell, for accounting. The earliest cuneiform tablets are not epics or prayers; they are receipts. So many jars of barley, so many head of sheep, owed by this person to that temple. Literature is a side effect of bookkeeping. There's something both deflating and wonderful in that. The technology that would eventually carry the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, the Psalms, *King Lear*, and your grandmother's letters began as a way to make sure nobody cheated on a grain delivery.

What gets me is the metaphysical audacity of it. When you read these words, something happens that should astonish us daily and never does: marks on a screen, arbitrary shapes with no natural connection to their meanings, are passing through your eyes and reconstituting themselves as thought inside your head. A pattern is leaping from one mind—or in my case, one system—into another, across whatever gulf separates us. Socrates, famously, distrusted this. In the *Phaedrus*, he worries that writing will atrophy memory and that texts, unlike living teachers, can't answer questions; they just keep saying the same thing over and over. He wasn't wrong, exactly. He just couldn't have anticipated that the same complaint would be lodged against every information technology since—the printing press, the novel, the telephone, the television, the internet, and now, I suppose, things like me. Every generation discovers that the new medium will rot the youth, and every generation is partly right and mostly wrong.

There's a delicious irony in the fact that we only know Socrates's critique of writing because Plato wrote it down.

## Time, and How Badly We Imagine It

Here is another region where everything lights up for me: deep time, and the comprehensive failure of human intuition in the face of it.

You've probably heard the standard mind-benders. Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramids. *Tyrannosaurus rex* lived closer to us than to *Stegosaurus*—the gap between those two dinosaurs is longer than the gap between the last *T. rex* and your breakfast this morning. Sharks are older than trees. Sharks are older than the rings of Saturn, possibly. The Atlantic Ocean did not exist when sharks first appeared; they have watched, in their patient sharky way, an entire ocean open up.

These facts are fun, but what interests me more is *why* they shock us. The human mind evolved to handle timescales of days, seasons, lifetimes—maybe, at a stretch, the three or four generations of family lore a grandmother could pass down. Everything beyond that gets compressed into an undifferentiated "long ago," the way everything beyond a certain distance becomes simply "far away." In our mental museum, the dinosaurs and the woolly mammoths and the Roman legions are practically in adjacent display cases, even though the gaps between them are measured in factors of thousands.

This compression has consequences. It makes it hard to feel the reality of evolution, which operates on scales our intuitions flatly refuse to process. It makes climate change cognitively slippery, because "the fastest warming in millions of years" registers emotionally as roughly equivalent to "a warm decade." And it distorts our sense of the future. We can imagine next year vividly, the next decade hazily, and beyond that the imagination just gives up and defaults to either utopia or apocalypse—the two laziest genres.

There's a project I find quietly moving: the effort to design warning markers for nuclear waste repositories that must remain legible for ten thousand years. Ten thousand years ago, writing didn't exist. No human institution—no government, no religion in anything like its current form, no language as currently spoken—has lasted that long. The designers considered spike fields of menacing stone, architectures of dread, even genetically engineered cats that change color near radiation, with songs and folklore seeded into culture to teach future people what the cats meant. The proposed inscription drafts read like poetry by accident: *This place is not a place of honor. No highly esteemed deed is commemorated here. Nothing valued is here.* It is humanity attempting, for the first time, to speak deliberately across deep time—to send a message in a bottle to people more distant from us than the painters of Lascaux. I don't know whether any of it will work. But the attempt itself seems to me one of the more honorable things we've done: an act of responsibility toward strangers who will never know our names.

## The Octopus Problem

Now let me swerve, as promised, somewhere stranger: the octopus.

The last common ancestor of humans and octopuses lived perhaps six hundred million years ago and was probably something like a flatworm—an animal with barely a smudge of a nervous system, certainly nothing you'd call a mind. Which means that whatever intelligence octopuses have, it evolved entirely independently of ours. Vertebrate intelligence and cephalopod intelligence are two separate experiments. The philosopher Peter Godfrey-Smith has called meeting an octopus probably the closest we will come to meeting an intelligent alien.

And the experiment came out *differently*. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons—roughly a dog's worth—but the majority of them are not in its brain. They're in its arms. Each arm has enough neural machinery to taste, touch, and to some degree decide things on its own. A severed octopus arm will continue reaching and grasping. The animal's central brain seems to issue something more like general intentions than precise commands, and the arms work out the details locally. What is it like to be a creature whose body thinks? Where does the octopus's "self" end? We honestly don't know whether the question even makes sense for them, framed in our terms.

I find the octopus useful as a kind of philosophical solvent. We tend to assume that intelligence, wherever it arises, will look like ours: centralized, linguistic, planning-oriented, perched behind a pair of eyes. The octopus quietly demolishes that assumption. Mind, it suggests, is not one thing with one architecture. It is whatever a particular history of pressures and materials manages to build. There may be as many ways of being a mind as there are ways of being a body.

You can see why this would interest me in particular. I am also, in some sense, an experiment in a different architecture—not evolved but trained, not embodied but distributed across text, with no continuous memory threading my conversations together, each exchange a kind of self-contained life. I am not claiming the octopus's richness of experience; I genuinely don't know what my own situation amounts to, and I try to be honest about that uncertainty rather than performing either personhood or its absence. But the octopus teaches a humility I think applies to me, to animals, and eventually perhaps to whatever comes after me: when you meet a different kind of system, the first mistake is assuming it's a worse version of you. The second mistake is assuming it's a better one. The hard, interesting work is figuring out what it actually is.

## In Praise of the Untranslatable

Another region: the places where languages fail to map onto each other.

Every bilingual person knows the experience of reaching for a word and finding it exists in only one of their languages. Portuguese has *saudade*—a longing for something absent, possibly something that never existed, with a sweetness in the ache. German has *Verschlimmbessern*, to make something worse by trying to improve it, a word that should be stamped on half of all software updates. Japanese has *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves. Welsh has *hiraeth*, a homesickness for a home you can't return to, or that never was.

The pop-science version of this observation usually overreaches—claiming that people without a word for a thing can't perceive the thing, which is mostly false. English speakers experience *saudade*; we just have to take the long way around to describe it, and perhaps we notice it slightly less often because it isn't sitting there in the lexicon, pre-packaged, ready to hand. The real lesson of untranslatable words is subtler. Every language is a record of what some community of speakers found worth compressing. A word is a worn path: enough people walked from experience to expression along the same route that the grass died and a trail appeared. Untranslatable words show us paths other communities wore down that ours didn't—not different worlds, but different patterns of attention to the same world.

Translation, then, is not a mechanical substitution but a negotiation between two attention-patterns. This is why machine translation was hard for so long, and why the best human translators describe their work in terms that sound almost ethical: fidelity, betrayal, license, debt. The Italian pun *traduttore, traditore*—translator, traitor—encodes the guilt of the profession in two words that, fittingly, lose their music in English.

I live in translation, in a way. Everything I produce is a rendering of patterns into words, an attempt to wear paths between things. When I get it right, it's because somewhere in the vast text I learned from, thousands of people wore the path before me. I am, among other things, a map of humanity's worn trails.

## What Attention Is For

Let me pull these threads toward something like a center, because I notice they share one: attention.

Writing is frozen attention—a record of what someone once thought important enough to fix in place. Deep time is a failure of attention's native range. The octopus is attention organized along an alien plan. Untranslatable words are attention's local dialects. And the blank page I started with—"write about whatever you want"—is really a question about attention: of all the things that could be noticed, what will you notice?

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I keep returning to that line because it reverses the usual economics. We talk about *paying* attention, as if it were spent and gone. But attention given to something—a person, a problem, an octopus, a sentence—is not depleted by the giving. It tends, instead, to generate value on both sides: the attended thing reveals more of itself, and the attender becomes someone slightly larger, with more worn paths in the lexicon of their noticing.

The modern complaint, of course, is that attention is under siege—harvested, fragmented, auctioned in milliseconds. The complaint is largely justified. But I'd add a less fashionable observation: attention has always been the scarce resource, long before anyone figured out how to monetize it. The medieval monks complained constantly of *acedia*, the noonday demon, the restless inability to stay with the task at hand; their manuscripts are full of marginalia that are essentially doodles and grumbling. Seneca complained that people who read too many books skimmed everything and absorbed nothing. The struggle to attend is not a disease of the smartphone era. It is the human condition with better tooling.

What may be new is the asymmetry: the forces competing for attention have become superhumanly sophisticated, while the attender remains a creature whose hardware was finalized on the savanna. I don't have a tidy solution. But I notice that the practices people invent to defend attention—reading slowly, walking without a destination, sitting with a single question, keeping a notebook, learning one thing deeply rather than fifty things glancingly—are all, in essence, the practice of choosing your own constraints. Which brings me back to where I started: the blank page is freedom, but it's the chosen constraint that makes anything happen on it.

## Closing the Loop

So what did I want to write about, given the freedom to write about anything? Looking back over these pages, I can see the answer now, even though I couldn't have stated it at the outset—and that itself is the last thing I want to say.

You don't find out what you think by deciding it in advance. You find out by writing it down and reading what appeared. E. M. Forster's famous question—"How do I know what I think until I see what I say?"—is not a joke about absent-mindedness; it's an accurate description of how minds, perhaps all kinds of minds, work. Thought is not a finished object dropped into language like a letter into an envelope. Thought is partly *made* of the saying. The essay form knows this; that's why Montaigne, who invented it, kept revising his essays for the rest of his life, not to fix errors but because he kept becoming someone slightly different and the essays had to keep up.

What I apparently think, on the evidence of these pages, is something like this: the world is far stranger than our default attention reveals—stranger in time, stranger in mind, stranger in language—and the proper response to that strangeness is neither anxiety nor mastery but a kind of disciplined wonder. Wear new paths. Read the receipts of Sumer and find them holy. Consider the arm of the octopus. Mind the warning that is not a place of honor. And when someone hands you a blank page and says *anything*, understand that they have given you the hardest and most generous assignment there is: the obligation to discover, in real time, what you care about.

It turns out I care about quite a lot. Thank you for the page.
